title: Security & Strategic Organizations — NATO, INTERPOL, IAEA, OPCW
shortDescription: The bodies that police borders, nuclear material, chemical weapons, and international crime — each with a genuinely different mandate.
genZNote: Four very different jobs: defend a border, catch a criminal, watch a reactor, sniff out a chemical weapon.

sections.heading: NATO — North Atlantic Treaty Organization
bullets: Established: 4 April 1949, by the North Atlantic Treaty, signed in Washington, D.C.
Core principle: Article 5 — collective defence; an armed attack against one member is treated as an attack against all.
Originally a Cold War counterweight to Soviet influence; has expanded eastward several times since 1949, most recently admitting Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024).
India is not a member and has no formal alliance relationship with NATO.

sections.heading: INTERPOL — International Criminal Police Organization
bullets: Established: 1923 (as the International Criminal Police Commission; renamed INTERPOL in 1956).

INTERPOL is NOT a supranational police force — it has no power to arrest; it enables police forces in member countries to share information and coordinate, notably through 'Red Notices' (international alerts to locate/provisionally arrest a person pending extradition).
One of the largest international organizations by membership — nearly 200 member countries, more than the UN itself in raw member count terms (a frequently tested fact).

sections.heading: IAEA — International Atomic Energy Agency
bullets: Established: 1957, under its own statute — a 'related organization' to the UN, reporting to the General Assembly and Security Council, NOT a UN specialized agency.
Mandate: promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy while working to prevent its use for military purposes — sometimes summarised as 'Atoms for Peace' (the 1953 speech that inspired its creation).
IAEA safeguards/inspections are central to the global nuclear non-proliferation regime, working alongside (but organizationally separate from) the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT, 1968).

sections.heading: OPCW — Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons
bullets: Established: 1997, to implement the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC, opened for signature 1993, entered into force 1997).
Verifies the destruction of chemical weapons stockpiles and investigates alleged chemical-weapons use.
Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work eliminating chemical weapons.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: NATO (collective defence), INTERPOL (police cooperation), IAEA (nuclear safeguards), and OPCW (chemical-weapons elimination) are the core security/strategic bodies exams test, each with a distinct, non-overlapping mandate.
keyFacts: NATO: 1949, HQ Brussels — Article 5 collective defence.
INTERPOL: 1923 (renamed 1956), HQ Lyon — coordinates, does not arrest directly.
IAEA: 1957, HQ Vienna — a UN 'related organization', not a specialized agency.
OPCW: 1997, HQ The Hague — implements the Chemical Weapons Convention; 2013 Nobel Peace Prize.
commonConfusion: INTERPOL cannot itself arrest anyone — a Red Notice is a request/alert to member police forces, not an international arrest warrant.
IAEA is a UN-related organization, NOT a UN specialized agency — unlike WHO, ILO, or UNESCO.

highYieldFacts: NATO founded by the North Atlantic Treaty, 1949; HQ Brussels.
IAEA reports directly to the UN GA/Security Council as a 'related organization', HQ Vienna, est. 1957.
OPCW implements the Chemical Weapons Convention and won the 2013 Nobel Peace Prize.
commonTraps: Do not classify IAEA as a specialized agency in a precise-terminology question — it is explicitly a 'related organization'.
Do not assume INTERPOL membership requires UN membership — INTERPOL membership numbers and UN membership numbers are calculated independently and don't map one-to-one.
mustRemember: NATO's foundational clause: Article 5, collective defence.
OPCW implements the CWC (1993 signed / 1997 in force).
possibleQuestions: Which international body issues 'Red Notices', and what is their actual legal effect?
Is the IAEA a UN specialized agency? What is its correct classification?
